content: Logical tests and automatically calculated fields, such as determining a patient's age from their date of birth, are essential tools for ensuring data accuracy. However, errors can still occur, and it is crucial to identify and address these by running queries on national datasets. While some errors can be prevented during data entry, others, such as implausible values, may still arise. For instance, a patient recorded in 2012 with a birthdate of January 1, 1848, is an example of an unrealistic value. Systems should define acceptable ranges for numeric and date fields and enforce these during data entry. Outliers and values outside these ranges should be identified through methods like frequency charts or distribution analysis. Duplicate records, where multiple entries refer to the same tuberculosis (TB) case, are another common issue. These can be identified using unique identifiers such as identity card numbers or social security numbers. De-duplication algorithms often rely on probabilistic matching of variables like name, sex, address, date of birth, and diagnosis date. These algorithms account for variations in spelling and recording and require high completeness rates for these fields. Potential duplicates identified by the system must be manually verified to confirm whether they represent the same TB case or separate cases. To assess data quality benchmarks, national TB surveillance systems should analyze records of notified TB cases, system documentation, and standard operating procedures (SOPs) for detecting and removing duplicates. Data quality checks should identify and correct misclassified, implausible, inconsistent, or missing data. If standard procedures are not in place, additional tests may be required. Running system-level data quality checks on national datasets for the assessment year is essential. This includes examining variables like age, sex, year of registration, bacteriological results, treatment history, and anatomical disease site. If feasible, the duplicate detection algorithm used by the country should be applied to the national dataset. In cases where de-duplication is a lengthy process involving both automated and manual checks, alternative methods, such as reviewing records of the de-duplication process or calculating the percentage of flagged potential duplicates, can be used. The main limitations of data quality assessments include variations in national database structures and data checks across countries. Duplicate cases can only be assessed in systems with sufficient patient-specific information, such as name, date of birth, and address. Some data entry errors, like incorrect birthdates, may not be detectable at the national level without source document verification. If standard data checking and correction procedures are in place, the first benchmark is satisfied. If less than 1% of records are flagged as potential duplicate TB cases, the third benchmark is satisfied. Meeting all benchmarks indicates that the standard is met. If only one or two benchmarks are satisfied, the standard is partially met. If the first benchmark is not satisfied, the standard is not met, regardless of the other benchmarks. Recommended actions for unmet standards include implementing data quality checks, providing feedback to sub-national users, highlighting data quality in regular meetings, developing SOPs and training materials, and securing senior management commitment to data quality. Cross-checking data between national and sub-national levels through site visits and establishing a national data management unit are additional options. Operational research can also help evaluate and improve data quality in surveillance systems. Examples of high-performing systems include the Netherlands, which uses a web-based TB notification system with built-in data validation routines to prevent implausible or inaccurate entries. Data managers review newly registered cases daily, and inconsistencies are sent back to local staff for clarification. The system satisfied all three benchmarks in 2011, meeting the standard. In the United Kingdom, Public Health England (PHE) manages a national web-based surveillance system that collects TB data in real-time. Mandatory fields like notification date and date of birth are 100% complete, and data validation checks prevent errors during entry. Quarterly reports identify data problems, and inconsistencies are followed up with clinics. The UK system satisfied two out of three benchmarks, partially meeting the standard. In the United States, 60 reporting areas use either CDC-generated software or their own systems to report TB cases. CDC applies 211 validation rules to submitted data and provides feedback to reporting areas. However, de-duplication is the responsibility of each jurisdiction, and the national dataset does not include patient names or addresses, making de-duplication at the national level challenging. The US system satisfied two out of three benchmarks, partially meeting the standard. The evaluation of external consistency in TB surveillance data involves comparing national data against plausible ranges based on global TB epidemiology. For example, a small proportion of TB cases typically occur among children. The percentage of cases among children can indicate recent infection rates and the performance of the surveillance system in capturing diagnosed cases. National surveillance data should be analyzed to determine the percentage of new TB cases among children under 15 years of age. If values fall within the stated ranges, the benchmark is satisfied, and the standard is met.
